Planets around other stars are far too faint to see directly, so astronomers detect them indirectly.
Let me describe the two most productive methods.
The transit method watches a star's brightness.
If a planet passes in front of the star, the star dims very slightly, and if that dimming repeats at regular intervals, we've probably found a planet.
The size of the dip tells us how big the planet is.
The second approach, the wobble method, looks for motion.
A planet's gravity pulls on its star, so the star moves back and forth a tiny bit.
That motion shifts the color of the star's light, and from that shift we can estimate the planet's mass.
Each method has blind spots, which is why the most reliable discoveries are confirmed by both.
Oh, and the first planet around a sun-like star was announced in 1995, which surprised many researchers at the time.
